content: The document discusses the safety of dolutegravir (DTG), a second-generation integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) antiretroviral drug, during pregnancy and breastfeeding. DTG has demonstrated improved virologic efficacy and tolerance compared to other antiretroviral therapies (ART). However, its effects during pregnancy were not studied in randomized controlled trials prior to its approval, as pregnancy was an exclusion criterion in phase 3 trials. Ongoing studies, such as DolPHIN-1/2 and IMPAACT 2010 (VESTED), are investigating DTG use in pregnancy, enrolling women after the first trimester. Published data on DTG use during pregnancy remain limited, with few studies examining its use at conception. A systematic review by Andrew Hill and colleagues for the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2018 identified six studies evaluating birth outcomes and pharmacokinetics of DTG in pregnancy. Additional data from the Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry (APR) and other studies have since been reviewed. The review excluded small studies with fewer than five participants or case reports. DTG is highly protein-bound and primarily metabolized through glucuronidation via the UGT1A1 enzyme, with minor contributions from CYP3A4. Neonates have low UGT1A1 and CYP3A4 activity at birth, potentially affecting DTG elimination acquired through placental transfer. However, studies on raltegravir, another INSTI metabolized by UGT1A1, showed minimal effects on neonatal bilirubin levels or clinical outcomes. No significant issues with hyperbilirubinemia in neonates exposed to DTG have been reported. Preclinical reproductive toxicity studies in rats and rabbits did not demonstrate adverse fertility, developmental outcomes, or teratogenicity at doses significantly higher than those used in humans. In human pregnancy, pharmacokinetic studies indicate that DTG plasma concentrations are lower during pregnancy compared to postpartum, with reductions in area under the curve (AUC) and trough concentrations during the third trimester. Despite these reductions, DTG levels remained above the inhibitory concentration (IC90), and viral suppression was achieved in most participants. Standard dosing of DTG (50 mg once daily) was deemed acceptable during pregnancy. Placental transfer of DTG is high, with a fetal-to-maternal ratio of approximately 60%. DTG was detectable in infants up to 7–9 days after birth, with prolonged half-life likely due to immature UGT1A1 enzyme activity. Breast milk transfer of DTG was low, with infant plasma levels below therapeutic targets but above the protein-adjusted IC90. No specific adverse events were reported in breastfeeding infants. Pregnancy outcomes, including stillbirth, spontaneous abortion, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age infants, were reviewed. The study reported an NTD prevalence of 0.12% with non-DTG ART and 0.09% in HIV-uninfected women. The defects included anencephaly, encephalocele, and myelomeningocele. Ongoing studies and surveillance efforts will provide additional data to guide clinical recommendations.
